q: Pictured: dowel. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Abang” is the vernacular for dowel. Native term; origin not confirmed. Memory hook: abang means “to wait”; the dowel waits hidden inside the joint.

q: Pictured: soldering bar (nicolite). Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Estanyo / Estaniyo” is the vernacular for soldering bar (nicolite). Origin: Spanish estaño “tin”, since solder is largely tin.

q: Pictured: groove. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Kanal / Canal” is the vernacular for groove. Origin: Spanish canal “channel”. A groove is a small channel cut in the wood.

q: Pictured: solder. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Hinang” is the vernacular for solder. Native Visayan word: hinang means “to work, make”. Memory hook: the tinsmith's work of joining metal.

q: Pictured: door or window jamb. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Hamba” is the vernacular for door or window jamb. Origin: Spanish jamba “jamb”. Filipino spelling turns j into h, as in jamba, hamba.

q: Pictured: iron. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Hiero” is the vernacular for iron. Origin: Spanish hierro “iron”, from Latin ferrum, the root of “ferrous”.

q: Pictured: butt hinge. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Bisagra” is the vernacular for butt hinge. Origin: Spanish bisagra “hinge”.

q: Pictured: wrench (labelled “anchor” in the source). Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Liyabe” is the vernacular for wrench (labelled “anchor” in the source). Origin: Spanish llave “key; wrench”. The source labels it “anchor”, but the picture shows wrenches and liyabe commonly means wrench, so treat the “anchor” label with caution.

q: Pictured: chain bolt. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Baral de Kadena” is the vernacular for chain bolt. Origin: kadena is Spanish cadena “chain”, and de is “of”, so the chain-type bolt.

q: Pictured: panel door. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “de Bandeha” is the vernacular for panel door. Origin: likely Spanish de bandeja “tray-like”. The recessed panels look like trays.

q: Pictured: window sill. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Pasamano” is the vernacular for window sill. Origin: Spanish pasamano, from pasar “to pass” + mano “hand”. It is a rail or ledge you run or rest your hand along.

q: Pictured: cabinet hinge. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Espolon” is the vernacular for cabinet hinge. Origin: Spanish espolón “spur”. Memory aid: the hinge sticks out from the cabinet like a spur.

q: Pictured: miter joint. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Canto Mesa / Kanto Mesa” is the vernacular for miter joint. Likely from Spanish canto “edge, corner” + mesa “table”: the neat corner joint of a table or frame.

q: Pictured: G.I. sheet strap. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Lingueta” is the vernacular for G.I. sheet strap. Origin: Spanish lengüeta “little tongue, tab”. A strap is a thin tongue of metal.
